content:
This is the record-breaking temperature of 36.9°C on August 9 of this year, and in Sheung Shui it shot up to 39.8°C in the early afternoon. In that extreme heat, I stayed indoors behind tightly shut windows with only a crack left for ventilation. I live on a mid-floor unit between two hills and avoid direct sunlight around noon; even without air-conditioning, the three ceiling fans whirred out cool breezes through the house. In Hong Kong's scorching summer, one has to learn gratitude.

I spent that hottest day on record washing clothes at home. Just past one in the afternoon I put two large bedsheets and duvet covers, four pairs of jeans and a pile of T-shirts into the machine. Two hours later I turned the sheets and covers inside out to dry again on the other side. After six in the evening I gathered up the warm laundry — it felt like it had just come out of a commercial washer-dryer at the laundromat — and laid it on the bed. I cannot remember the last time I had clothes dried naturally so cleanly under the sun. I should have been worrying about a friend under the blazing sun; all I could do was run load after load and try to offset the sun's ferocity, if only a little.

August has become a recurring nightmare. I do not know how many more times it will take before I can break free from this loop of summer partings. In a dream one night, I strutted along arm in arm with my mother, saying proudly, 'My little mummy,' gripping her tightly with great joy. Then I saw ahead of us a mysterious woman in a long, deep maroon cloak. I instinctively did not want to see her face, but the dream kept zooming in — she was a strange woman I did not recognise. When I woke, the smug, elated feeling welled up, and what stayed with me was simply this: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of 10 August 2020, our family sang hymns and kissed my mother's forehead to bid her farewell — it was a full stop. Yet learning to let go is a lesson one never truly masters in a lifetime. Not letting go is a wound that runs quietly deep. Six years on, regrets still surface in countless small details; in my mind I keep replaying the days that led to that one.

The regrets and reluctance of parting will surface sooner or later, at any age. A female student in my writing class wrote about her late grandmother. It was a piece of remembrance, mourning and regret. When she was even younger, she had resented living in the countryside with her grandmother; during the day she would bicker with the old lady with the boundless energy of a little imp. When her grandmother tweaked her ear, she would hit back so the old woman could feel the same pain she felt. Then, peering through the crack of a door, the little girl saw her doddering grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever and, dazed, walked up to her grandmother and said: 'I feel awful.'

Feeling awful simply means feeling unwell — it is how a child experiences sickness. She had a high fever and her whole body was burning. Without a word, her grandmother found clean clothes, changed her, and immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to queue for the doctor. That medicinal-oil smell she had always found so repulsive carried her to the hospital in a haze. Before long, for some reason, the smell faded, and the little girl found herself sitting alone near the reception desk waiting. Then a few adults asked her: 'Where's your family?' As she spoke she began to cry — until the medicinal-oil scent drifted close again, and she settled down and waited calmly to see the doctor for an injection and medicine.

Back home, the medicinal-oil smell was as usual, but its sharpness seemed to have gone. From the kitchen came the rhythmic chopping on a board, and from the pot the warm fragrance of rice porridge. The essentials of life on earth need no elaborate explanation — it is really this simple, this clear.

I wonder — today, when one is ill, who is it that cooks the porridge?

When I was small, it was mostly my father, sometimes my mother, who had the patience to chop beef by hand to make congee for me. This was the sick-day menu, and I was the only one who got to eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this meat congee: 'I want a beef and scallion congee.' It was the privilege of being ill. Now, no one makes this particular congee for me anymore; when I am sick, I will never again eat this kind of beef congee.

'These days, if you're ill, just call FoodPanda,' a friend said. Other friends cook plain congee or fish congee for their wives. 'Sometimes I make minced-meat congee too.' 'Hand-chopped, mind you, not blended in a food processor.' 'Takes only a few minutes to chop.' A pot of congee makes one feel treasured.

'In a lifetime, not many people will cook congee for you when you fall ill. Once you grow up, the most likely scenario is that you will be the one cooking for others. Most people have been through this. Whatever you are feeling, take a proper farewell, say what is in your heart. Anyone reading it will find some peace.' I told the student. She looked at me, a flicker of light in her eyes.

A piece of writing about a grandmother can bring peace. My father, my mother, my grandmother — these are stories we know instinctively how to write.

The student was not merely a good writer; she seized on the medicinal oil as the central thread and, building around it, conveyed her true feelings about her closest relative. She may not have been the one who loved her grandmother most, but that time together, arranged by fate, made it impossible for her today to forget all that her grandmother had done for her — nor to fail to see that people simply grow up that way, without quite knowing how. In the end, she turned in a deeply moving piece that left one feeling, quite literally, 'unwell.'

The medicinal oil went from being hated, to being reliable, to being a source of shame, and finally became something to be remembered. It turned out that on her very first day of primary school, the girl had been laughed at by classmates for smelling of the oil — they had called her a country bumpkin. She ran home crying and loudly ordered her grandmother to wash every single piece of clothing from top to bottom with lots of washing powder. The grandmother had clutched the laundry and wept. The grandmother had been looking after her from the age of eight months, right up until she grew up and went to school and was exposed to the wider world; the granddaughter had become like a different person, and had hurt her grandmother's heart. After she went back to live with her mother, a day came when the grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The student went back with her mother to visit, only to find that she was no longer 'recognised.'

'You can't be my granddaughter — she doesn't like talking to me,' the old grandmother told her.

Life is so real, and so cruel. Have I ever treated my own mother this cruelly? Perhaps not. Or perhaps I have, and like the student, I simply do not know. Family members sometimes hurt one another. The point is, from here on, will we come to understand love more deeply?
